name: William Blake
summary: Blake was an English poet and engraver who wrote against institutional religion, state power and war, and for imagination and energy over reason. His own words attack priests, kings and penal law and welcome the fall of tyrants, but he left no programme on most modern political questions.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Song of Liberty welcomes the fall of kings and calls on France to rend down her dungeon, but it is symbolic prophecy and not a stated rule for when revolution is justified.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: In his rewritten Lord's Prayer he asks that money, debt, tax, value or price be taken away since all things are held in common.

war-builds-character.rationale: Against Bacon's praise of war for a state's greatness he asks whether virtue means war and its horrors and heroic villains, and answers that this is neither great nor Christian.

separate-church-state.rationale: Blake calls state religion the source of all cruelty and rejects codes given under pretence of divine command; Britannica notes he abominated institutionalized religion, especially when allied with government.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: In the Watson annotations he calls the laws of the Jews the basest and most oppressive of human codes, given under pretence of divine command, and says all penal laws are cruelty; the Song of Liberty has the stony law stamped to dust.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell proverb calls setting another before you the most sublime act.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The Song of Liberty chorus and Visions of the Daughters of Albion both close with everything that lives is holy; he also writes that where man is not nature is barren.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Annotating Bacon he writes that a state grows by internal improvement and that states are not improved at the expense of foreigners.

universal-morality.rationale: He writes that conscience in those that have it is unequivocal, that virtue is not opinion and that virtue and honesty are of no doubtful signification to anyone.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He writes that rational truth is the truth of Pilate, not of Christ, that reasoning is nothing against downright plain truth, and that Bacon put an end to faith.

clerical-rule.rationale: In the Marriage of Heaven and Hell he says priesthood began when some enslaved the vulgar by turning poetic deities into commands, and in the Watson annotations he calls priests inquisitors, rejecting rule by clergy.

death-penalty.rationale: He writes that all penal laws court transgression and are therefore cruelty and murder, which excludes executions as a penalty.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: He holds that all penal laws court transgression and are cruelty and murder, which includes a penalty for leaving a religion.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Auguries of Innocence treats the suffering of caged birds, hunted hares, misused horses and oxen and the wounded lark as wrongs that cry to heaven.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: He holds that all penal laws court transgression and are cruelty and murder, which includes making a sexual act a criminal offence.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: He holds that all penal laws are cruelty and murder; he also wrote that defending the Bible would then cost a man his life, treating religious censorship as persecution.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: He calls the Israelites' killings under pretence of divine command abominable, says the Scriptures show human wickedness as examples and that the Bible's divinity is in its sentiments, not its historical record.

national-church-status.rationale: Blake writes that State Religion is the abomination that is the source of all cruelty, so he rejects a favoured legal status for a national church.

notes: Searched every theme in the statement list against Blake's marginalia, the Marriage of Heaven and Hell, the Songs and Auguries of Innocence. His positions cluster on religion, law and war; economy, government structure, immigration, ecology policy and technology are null because he never spoke to them as such. Jerusalem, America, Europe and The Four Zoas were not found in full text, so statements they might settle stay null. A repeated line in the Watson annotations that all penal laws are cruelty and murder answers the four statements on punishing offences. His later turn from revolutionary hope is reported only by secondary accounts, so the revolution answer is low. The audit is expected to fail the uncertainty rule.
